history.heading: Cradle of Polynesia
paragraphs: Samoa, in the South Pacific, was settled around 3,000 years ago by people of the Lapita culture. It is often considered a cradle of Polynesian culture. Samoan society developed around extended families led by chiefs (matai), and powerful families held paramount titles.

European contact increased in the 19th century, and missionaries converted most Samoans to Christianity. Rivalry between Germany, Britain and the United States led to the 1899 division: the western islands became German Samoa, and the eastern islands American Samoa.

history.heading: Mau movement and independence
paragraphs: New Zealand took Western Samoa in 1914. Poor handling of the 1918 influenza pandemic killed about a fifth of the population. The non-violent Mau movement demanded independence; on Black Saturday in 1929, police killed its leader, Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III. New Zealand apologised in 2002.

Western Samoa became independent on 1 January 1962, the first Pacific island nation to do so. It changed its name to Samoa in 1997. In 2011 it moved west of the International Date Line, skipping 30 December.

culture.heading: Fa'a Samoa
paragraphs: Samoan and English are official languages. Life follows fa'a Samoa, the Samoan way, centred on family, chiefs, church and respect. Most land is customarily owned. Christianity is central, and Sunday is strictly observed.
Traditional tattooing (tatau), the siva dance and the fire-knife dance are famous. Food is cooked in an umu (earth oven). Rugby is a national passion, with the Manu Samoa team.

politics.heading: Parliamentary democracy
paragraphs: Samoa is a parliamentary democracy in which only matai (chiefs) can stand for most seats in parliament. The head of state is elected by parliament. In 2021 Fiamē Naomi Mata'afa became the first female prime minister after a constitutional crisis ended decades of rule by the Human Rights Protection Party. Politics shifted again after elections in 2025.

economy.heading: Small island economy
paragraphs: Samoa's economy relies on remittances from Samoans in New Zealand, Australia and the US, tourism, agriculture (coconut products, taro and nonu) and fishing. Development aid is important. The currency is the tala.
